h2: Introduction to NDT course: what Level 1 training starts with
html:
Many people searching for an introduction to NDT course want to know whether NDT suits them before committing to a method. The practical answer is that Level 1 training is the introduction. The first course in a method teaches the basics of nondestructive testing in general and then the method itself, and its hours count toward Level I (Level 1) certification under your employer's written practice.

What an introduction to NDT covers

  • Why NDT exists: finding discontinuities without damaging the part, and the difference between a discontinuity, an indication and a defect.
  • The main methods and what each finds: visual, penetrant and magnetic particle for surface flaws; ultrasonic and radiographic for internal flaws and thickness; eddy current for conductive materials and tubing.
  • Materials and processes: how welding, casting and forging create typical flaws, and how service creates corrosion, fatigue and cracking.
  • Codes, procedures and acceptance criteria, and why a Level I works to a written procedure rather than making acceptance decisions.
  • Safety, including radiation safety awareness for radiography.

Which method to start with

For most US entrants the first certifications are the surface methods, PT and MT, often with VT, because they need fewer training and experience hours and are used on almost every fabrication and maintenance job. UT is the method employers in oil, gas, power and fabrication most often ask for next. The guide on which NDT method to learn first works through the choice by industry.

NDT technician training and NDT inspector training

In NDT job listings, technician and inspector usually mean the same person: someone certified to perform a method. In the API world an inspector is someone else, a person certified by API to inspect pressure vessels, piping or tanks, which is a separate route with its own examinations and experience rules; the API inspection guides explain it. Level 1 NDT technician training is the start of the first route.

After the introduction

Level I certification still needs documented experience hours, your employer's general, specific and practical examinations, and a vision examination. Once you are working as a Level I, the next step is NDT Level 2 training. To start, ask the training team which course fits the job you are aiming for, or try the free practice tests.
